analysis.one_liner: Redirects Social Security payroll taxes into personal investment accounts run by private money managers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 2005, sent to the Ways and Means Committee's Social Security subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would convert Social Security into a system of individual investment accounts. Workers born in 1984 or later would automatically have their 6.2% employee payroll contribution deposited into a personal account invested in stocks and bonds, and workers born between 1951 and 1983 could choose to join. Participants would give up accruing traditional Social Security benefits on future wages (disability benefits excepted), and traditional benefits for everyone else would grow more slowly because benefit formulas would be indexed to prices instead of wages. Retirement income would come from the account through annuities or scheduled withdrawals, with a poverty-level minimum benefit as a floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who join would own an account invested in equities and bonds, could pass it to heirs tax-free at death, and could draw retirement income as an annuity or programmed withdrawals, with a supplemental benefit guaranteeing at least a poverty-level income. Financial firms would gain a very large new business: professional asset managers would be contracted to invest contributions, and retirees would buy annuities from Board-certified issuers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Younger workers and the financial industry

how_it_helps.text: Participating workers would have 100% of their 6.2% employee Social Security contribution deposited into a personal investment account held in trust for them, rather than paid into the shared trust fund.

Contributions would be invested with professional asset managers, with a default mix of 60% stocks and 40% bonds, and once a participant's balance passed $10,000 they could direct money into individually managed Tier III accounts.

Account balances and Tier I assets would be paid to a participant's named beneficiaries or estate in a lump sum upon death, something traditional Social Security survivor benefits do not do in that form.
Funds, accounts, annuities, and recognition bonds under the program would be exempt from federal income tax, and distributions would be excluded from gross income.

Participants whose account could not fund a poverty-level annuity would be entitled to a supplemental minimum benefit paid from the general fund, with a sliding scale for workers with few quarters of coverage.
Workers electing the new system would receive a recognition bond equal to the actuarial value of benefits they had already earned under the old system, redeemable at retirement age.

analysis.who_pays: If enacted, the changeover would be expensive: the government would issue recognition bonds (new federal debt backed by full faith and credit) to cover already-earned benefits, appropriate general-fund money for supplemental minimum benefits and to keep the trust funds solvent, and forgo tax revenue on the accounts. Participants would give up guaranteed benefit accrual on future wages, and traditional beneficiaries would face slower benefit growth because benefit formulas would be indexed to consumer prices rather than wage growth.

drawbacks.text: Participants would stop earning traditional Social Security benefits on wages after electing (disability benefits excepted), so their guaranteed, inflation-protected benefit would be replaced by whatever their investments produced.

For non-disability beneficiaries, the bill would switch benefit calculations from indexing to average wages to indexing to consumer prices; since wages historically rise faster than prices, this would cut the growth of traditional benefits for people staying in the old system.

Recognition bonds issued to new participants would be obligations of the United States backed by its full faith and credit, adding to federal debt during a long transition while payroll taxes were diverted into accounts.
A participant's supplemental minimum benefit would be reduced dollar-for-dollar by any need-based cash benefit such as SSI, which would offset the promised floor for the poorest retirees.

Administrative expenses of the investment funds and accounts would be deducted from participants' balances, reducing net returns, and retirees could only buy annuities from issuers certified by the new Board.
The election to join would be irrevocable, locking participants into market risk with no return to the traditional system.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but conditional: workers would own assets, could leave them to heirs, and would likely earn more over a long career if markets performed well, with a poverty-level guarantee underneath. The costs are certain: a large transition burden on the Treasury, slower benefit growth for everyone remaining in the traditional system, fee deductions from every account, and the loss of the guaranteed benefit formula that Social Security currently provides. Critics of privatization argued the plan traded a secure benefit for market risk and new fees; supporters argued individual ownership was worth it. The bill's own design acknowledges the risk by building a general-fund minimum benefit back in.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee in February 2005 and sent to its Social Security subcommittee two weeks later, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or vote until that Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Sam Johnson introduced the Individual Social Security Investment Program Act on February 2, 2005, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
On February 14, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Social Security; the record shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action afterward.
Johnson delivered introductory remarks on the measure twice, on February 1 and July 12, 2005, but the bill never advanced beyond the subcommittee.
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and bills that do not pass both chambers die at the end of a Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers keeping the traditional guaranteed Social Security benefit were left unchanged, and the asset-management and insurance industries never gained the new mandatory fee and annuity business the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Traditional Social Security; no new industry fees

for.name: Rep. Sam Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it twice in 2005.

for.name: 15 of 232 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Made creating personal Social Security accounts the centerpiece of his 2005 domestic agenda, campaigning nationwide for private accounts after his State of the Union address.

against.name: Rep. Bill Thomas
against.role: Chairman, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee never marked up the bill or reported it out; after referral to the Social Security subcommittee, no further action appears in the record.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for Social Security
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on February 2, 2005, and referred it to the Subcommittee on Social Security on February 14, 2005; it died there.

against.name: House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Opposed private-account Social Security legislation across the board in 2005, leaving the bill without any Democratic support.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 15 cosponsors were Republicans, no Democrat cosponsored, and Democrats uniformly opposed personal-account proposals during the 2005 Social Security debate.

industries.industry: Asset management and mutual fund firms
industries.note: The bill would have made contracted professional asset managers the permanent channel for Social Security contributions, creating a huge guaranteed business. Participants' balances would bear administrative expense deductions, so part of the industry's gain would come out of workers' returns.

Retirees could only convert their account balances to lifetime income through annuities issued by Board-certified insurers, a captive market for the industry, though issuers would face Board qualification and cost-of-living-adjustment requirements.
They would qualify as trustees for Tier III individual investment accounts, gaining new trust business from participants' balances.
